lesson.subtitle: Lesson 8 -- Overrated or Worth It
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ricardo Wertheim | Lesson 8 -- Overrated or Worth It
lesson.grammar_point: modal verbs should, could and might for advice, possibility and speculation

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: the only one of its kind, with nothing else like it
to give reasons for or against an idea, with someone who disagrees
not as good as most people say it is
to think about a decision again and possibly change it
good enough to justify the time, the money or the effort
normal or usual for a place or a group of people
the way one person sees a situation, from where they stand
away from the places most tourists go

paras: Every summer somebody writes that Dubrovnik is overrated. Too many people, too many cruise ships, too many restaurants with photographs on the menu. And every summer somebody answers that the walls are unique, that there is no second version of them anywhere in Europe, and that anyone who disagrees has never seen the stone at eight in the morning.

I think both sides are right, and that is exactly why people still argue about it. If you arrive at noon in August, you might see nothing but shoulders and umbrellas, and you could easily decide that the whole city is a museum for tourists. The same street at seven in the morning is empty and warm and completely yours. The city has not changed. Only your perspective has.

So my advice is simple: you should not ask whether a famous place is overrated. You should ask when it is worth it. Go early, stay two nights instead of one, and give yourself one afternoon off the beaten track, in the villages behind the coast, where lunch is typical, slow and half the price. If a place disappoints you, it might be the hour and not the place. And you could always reconsider it later, from a quieter street.

bank.label: Useful sentences for holding an opinion
items: In my opinion, the walls alone make the trip worth it.
I am not sure I agree -- I think the hour matters more than the place.
That is a fair point, but I would still go in June rather than August.
Have you considered that it might be the crowds and not the city?
You should go early, before the first boat arrives.
We could take the ferry instead, and it might be quieter.
From my perspective, the villages behind the coast are the real find.
I thought it was overrated at first, but now I would reconsider.

items.situation: Recommend one place off the beaten track, and say why it is not typical.

listenings.text: People ask me all the time whether the old town is overrated, and I never give the same answer twice. In August, honestly, it might be. You should see it at eight in the morning instead, when the shops are still closed and the stone is completely yours. My real advice is different, though. Give the coast two days, and then take the bus inland for one. Almost nobody does it. The villages up there are not unique in any dramatic way, but lunch is typical, it lasts three hours, and it costs half of what you pay by the water. That is the day people remember. Everything else they could have seen in a photograph.

I will argue the other side, because somebody has to. A place is not overrated simply because many people go there. The walls of Dubrovnik are unique, and there is no second version of them anywhere in Europe. What people really mean, I think, is that the experience is crowded, and that is a different complaint. So my honest opinion is this: you should pay for the guided walk at opening time. It costs more, it starts too early, and you might be tired. But you will stand on that stone with maybe thirty other people instead of three thousand, and then you can decide for yourself. Reconsider the hour, not the place.

extra_audio.text: First he read an article saying that the old town was overrated and not worth it any more. Then he went at noon in August and almost agreed, because he could hardly walk. The next morning he came back at seven and found the same street completely empty. That afternoon he took the bus inland, off the beaten track, and had a typical lunch that lasted three hours. In the end he reconsidered his whole opinion, and told his friends that the place was fine and the hour was the problem.
